questions.stem: A nurse obtains an unexpectedly high blood pressure reading on a client. Which factor could falsely elevate the reading?

opts.t: Using a cuff that is too small (narrow) for the client's arm
opts.r: A cuff that is **too small/narrow** for the arm gives a **falsely high** reading. (A cuff too large reads falsely low.)

opts.t: Positioning the arm at the level of the heart
opts.r: Arm at heart level is the **correct** technique and yields an accurate reading.

opts.t: Allowing the client to rest quietly for five minutes first
opts.r: Resting quietly first prevents falsely high readings — good technique.

opts.t: Using a cuff that covers about 80% of the upper arm circumference
opts.r: A properly sized cuff (bladder covering ~80% of the arm) is correct and improves accuracy.

questions.tip: Cuff-size errors: **too small → too high; too big → too low.** Also, an arm **below** heart level reads high; **above** heart level reads low.
questions.pearl: "**Small cuff, big number.**" When a value surprises you, **recheck technique before treating the number.**

questions.stem: A nurse is setting up a sterile field for a bedside procedure. Which action breaks sterile technique and requires the nurse to start over?

opts.t: Holding sterile items above waist level and within view
opts.r: Keeping sterile items **above the waist and in sight** maintains sterility.

opts.t: Considering the outer one-inch border of the sterile drape contaminated
opts.r: The **outer 1-inch border** of a sterile field is treated as **contaminated** — standard practice.

opts.t: Reaching across the sterile field to place an item on the far side
opts.r: **Reaching across a sterile field** contaminates it — the unsterile arm passes over sterile items. The nurse must set up so items are reached from the side, not over the top.

opts.t: Opening the outermost flap of a sterile package away from the body first
opts.r: Opening the **first flap away** from the body prevents reaching over the sterile contents.

questions.tip: Sterile rules to bank: **keep it in sight, above the waist; 1-inch border is dirty; never turn your back on it; never reach across it; wet = contaminated.**
questions.pearl: "**Below the waist or out of sight = it isn't sterile — not quite.**" When in doubt, throw it out and restart.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to give medication through a newly inserted nasogastric (NG) tube. Which method is the most reliable for verifying correct tube placement?

opts.t: Auscultating air injected into the tube over the stomach
opts.r: The **air/auscultation ("whoosh") test is unreliable** — sounds can transmit even if the tube is in the lung. It's no longer recommended as confirmation.

opts.t: Checking that the client is not coughing
opts.r: Absence of coughing does not confirm gastric placement; a tube can be misplaced without coughing.

opts.t: Reviewing the X-ray obtained after insertion
opts.r: **Radiographic (X-ray) confirmation** is the **gold standard** for verifying placement after initial insertion, before using the tube.

opts.t: Confirming the external tube length looks about right
opts.r: External length is a rough check for migration, not proof of correct initial placement.

questions.tip: For **initial** NG placement, the answer is **X-ray.** Ongoing checks may use **pH of aspirate** and measuring the external length — but never the air-auscultation method as confirmation.
questions.pearl: "**When in doubt, X-ray it out.**" Gastric aspirate is usually **acidic (pH ≤ 5)**; respiratory/intestinal fluid is more alkaline.

questions.stem: A confused older adult is at high risk for falls. The nurse plans care to keep the client safe. Which intervention should the nurse implement first?

opts.t: Apply a vest restraint to keep the client in bed.
opts.r: Restraints are a **last resort**, require an order, and can increase injury — not a first-line fall strategy.

opts.t: Place the bed in the lowest position with the call light in reach and initiate frequent rounding.
opts.r: The **least restrictive** measures come first: **low bed, call light within reach, nonslip footwear, a clear path, bed/chair alarms, and frequent (hourly) rounding.**

opts.t: Raise all four side rails to prevent the client from getting up.
opts.r: **Four raised side rails are considered a restraint** and can cause serious injury if the client climbs over.

opts.t: Keep the room dark and quiet at all times to reduce stimulation.
opts.r: A completely dark room can increase confusion and fall risk; some soft lighting aids orientation.

questions.tip: Always choose the **least restrictive** safe option first. Restraints and four side rails are **restraints** — near the bottom of the list, never the first answer.
questions.pearl: "**Least restrictive, first and best.**" Restraints need an **order, a time limit, and regular checks** — never PRN, never for staff convenience.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for a client with *Clostridioides difficile* (C. diff) infection. Which infection-control action is correct?

opts.t: Use alcohol-based hand sanitizer after removing gloves.
opts.r: **Alcohol sanitizer does not kill C. diff spores** — soap and water friction is required to physically remove them.

opts.t: Wash hands with soap and water, and use contact precautions with gown and gloves.
opts.r: C. diff requires **contact precautions (gown and gloves)** and **handwashing with soap and water.** Dedicated equipment and bleach-based cleaning are also used.

opts.t: Place the client on airborne precautions with an N95 respirator.
opts.r: C. diff spreads by contact/fecal-oral, **not airborne** — an N95 is unnecessary.

opts.t: No special precautions are needed if the client uses a private bathroom.
opts.r: Precautions are absolutely required; a private bathroom does not replace contact isolation.

questions.tip: Remember the "spore rule": for **C. diff (and norovirus)**, use
questions.pearl: "**Spores need soap.**" Match the bug to the precaution: **Contact** (C. diff, MRSA), **Droplet** (flu, meningitis, pertussis), **Airborne** (**M**easles, **T**B, **V**aricella — "**My Chicken Hez TB**").

questions.stem: A registered nurse (RN) is delegating tasks to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) on a busy med-surg unit. Which task is appropriate for the RN to delegate to the UAP?

opts.t: Performing the admission assessment on a new client
opts.r: **Assessment** is an RN responsibility and cannot be delegated.

opts.t: Recording the intake and output of a stable client
opts.r: Recording **intake and output** for a **stable** client is a routine, standardized task within the UAP's scope.

opts.t: Teaching a client how to use an incentive spirometer for the first time
opts.r: **Teaching** (client education) is an RN function, especially first-time instruction.

opts.t: Adjusting the flow rate of a client's IV fluids
opts.r: Titrating/adjusting IV fluids involves nursing judgment and is not delegated to a UAP.

questions.tip: UAPs handle **stable, routine, standard** tasks — vitals, hygiene, feeding, ambulating, I&O. The RN keeps the **"AT-E"**: **A**ssess,
questions.pearl: "**If it takes a nurse's brain, it stays with the nurse.**" Delegate the **stable and predictable**, keep the **unstable and the teaching.**
